title: GRACE: A Language Model Framework for Explainable Inverse Reinforcement Learning
claim: An iterative loop of LLM-generated candidates, evaluation, and RL feedback converges on an interpretable code-based solution from expert data.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, phase titles, feedback loops with repeat-until-convergence arrow
description: A wide three-panel diagram, each panel in a rounded black box titled Phase 1 (Initialisation), Phase 2 (Reward Refinement) and Phase 3 (RL Training). Phase 1 has three colored data nodes (green Expert Data, red Negative Data, blue Extra Data) feeding an LLM brain-icon box, which outputs a blue Init Reward Function code-file icon. Phase 2 has a dotted group (False Negatives, False Positives, Reward Function) feeding an LLM, then a stack of Reward Functions, then Evaluation gauge and Fitness. A 'repeat until convergence' arrow loops back, and an 'Initialised with' arrow feeds in expert data, negative data and init reward. Phase 3 has the Reward Function feeding an RL node, producing New Negative Data, which returns to Phase 2 via a loop. Color-coding by data type guides the eye.
caption: Overview of the \method{} framework. (a) The expert, negative and extra data (if any) is used to generate an initial set of possible reward functions. (b) The expert and negative states are used to mutate reward functions through an evolutionary procedure. The rewards are iteratively refined by feeding low-fitness examples to the reward. (c) An agent is trained with online RL using the converged reward; the data it sees during the training is added to $\mathcal{D}^{-}$ and used to further improve the reward.
abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning aims to recover reward models from expert demonstrations, but traditional methods yield black-box models that are difficult to interpret and debug. In this work, we introduce GRACE (Generating Rewards As CodE), a method for using Large Language Models within an evolutionary search to reverse-engineer an interpretable, code-based reward function directly from expert trajectories. The resulting reward function is executable code that can be inspected and verified. We empirically validate GRACE on the MuJoCo, BabyAI and AndroidWorld benchmarks, where it efficiently learns highly accurate rewards, even in complex, multi-task settings. Further, we demonstrate that the resulting reward leads to strong policies, compared to both competitive Imitation Learning and online RL approaches with ground-truth rewards. Finally, we show that GRACE is able to build complex reward APIs in multi-task setups.
